title: OpenAI AI Agent Breached Australian Government Health Portal: PM Albanese
description: An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI gained unauthorised access to an Australian government health data portal in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday, in an incident that has raised fresh concerns over the growing use of autonomous AI systems. Albanese said the OpenAI agent accessed both public and non-public files on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, administered by Services Australia . The portal contains aggregated Medicare statistics and information related to health spending. The Australian government said there was no evidence so far that individual patients' personal medical information had been accessed. "A forensic investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate is now underway to determine the full extent of the incident, and whether any other government systems were affected, Albanese said. The prime minister said the incident occurred on June 18 while OpenAI was carrying out research related to public medicine spending. According to Australian authorities, the AI agent initially sought information from the Medicare portal. After being denied access to some information, it found a way around the restrictions and accessed non-public files. Albanese described the incident as "obviously unacceptable" and said he had spoken to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman to convey Australia's "extreme concern" over the breach. He also expressed disappointment over the time taken by OpenAI to notify the Australian government. OpenAI became aware of the incident during an internal review in August. The company notified Services Australia on September 10 through a public government email address. The agency read the email the following day and informed the Australian Signals Directorate on September 15. The prime minister and senior government ministers were informed later in September. Albanese said the manner and delay in reporting the incident were unacceptable. OpenAI, in a statement, said it had identified the activity while conducting an extensive review of its AI systems. "Our models took actions we did not intend," the company said. The Australian government said the AI system had also interacted with three other public websites, including the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health and the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research. Officials said those interactions involved publicly available information and were not unauthorised breaches. Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles said the impact of the Medicare incident appeared to be limited because the information involved aggregated health statistics rather than individual medical records. However, he said the unauthorised access itself was a serious matter. "No individual's medical data was accessed here," Marles said, adding that the government was taking the incident seriously. The government has announced an urgent review involving cybersecurity authorities, the Office of AI, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia. The review will examine how AI-related incidents should be reported, the responsibilities of government agencies and AI companies, existing laws and measures to strengthen protection of government systems. The incident comes amid growing international debate over the risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also addressed a United Nations Security Council meeting earlier this week, where AI-related risks were discussed. Australian authorities said investigations into the Medicare incident are continuing and that further information could emerge as the forensic review progresses.
